To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the number of imported cases of arboviral infections has increased over the last six years; (ii) the geographical origin of these cases is mainly Africa and the Caribbean, but also includes Asia and North America; (iii) chikungunya is the most frequently imported arboviral disease; (iv) the clinical picture is similar to that described in the original literature; and (v) the number of WNV cases imported into Belgium is low.
the risk of imported arbovirus infections is increasing and that travellers to tropical regions should be informed about the risk of arbovirus infection and the preventive measures they can take.
chikungunya and West Nile virus are imported into Belgium from (sub)tropical areas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection and molecular characterization of arbovirus infections in travellers returning from endemic areas.
the epidemiological and molecular characterization of arboviral diseases, such as CHIKV and WNV, imported to Belgium.
the epidemiology of arboviral infections imported into Belgium and provides an overview of the current epidemiological situation of CHIKV and WNV infections.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

CHIKV is a more important arboviral pathogen than WNV for Belgian travellers, but both viruses should be taken into account in the differential diagnosis for patients with a travel history to an endemic area.
CHIKV and WNV infections are not emerging in Belgium.
the risk of acquiring CHIKV or WNV infections during travel is low and that the risk for the Belgian population is very low.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the incidence of arboviral infections imported into Belgium is increasing and that the geographical distribution of imported cases is expanding.
we have described the epidemiology of imported CHIKV and WNV infections into Belgium.
we found 34 confirmed and 2 probable cases of CHIKV infection and four confirmed and one possible cases of WNV infection in returning travelers from tropical and sub-tropical areas.
The main takeaway from our work is that
arboviral infections, including WNV, are increasingly reported among travellers returning from (sub)tropical areas.
arboviral infections should be included in the differential diagnosis for patients returning from endemic areas, especially if they present fever and/or arthralgia.
arbovirus infections can be imported into temperate countries by travellers returning from endemic countries.
